title: Jacob Misiorowski Leads NL Cy Young Race with Unanimous BBWAA Selection】
body:
Milwaukee’s right‑hander Jacob Misiorowski has clinched the National League Cy Young Award with a clean‑sweep of the Baseball Writers’ Association of America vote, becoming only the second Brewer ever to capture the honor for a NL pitcher. The 27‑year‑old’s dominant 2024 campaign—highlighted by a sub‑2.90 ERA, 242 strikeouts and a league‑leading 12 complete games—earned him unanimous recognition from all 30 BBWAA voters, a rare feat that underscores the historic nature of his performance.

Misiorowski’s ascent to the sport’s highest individual accolade began early in the season, when he posted a 1.85 ERA over his first 12 starts, striking out an average of 11.2 batters per nine innings while limiting walks to just 2.1 per nine. His ability to command a deep, late‑life slider and a sinker that induces weak contact made him a nightmare for opposing lineups. By the All‑Star break, he had already amassed 150 strikeouts, a figure that placed him atop the NL leaderboard and signaled that he was on a trajectory unlike any other pitcher in recent memory.

The unanimous vote places Misiorowski in an elite company. Only a handful of pitchers—most notably Sandy Koufax (1963), Pedro Martínez (1999) and Jacob de Grom (2018)—have ever received every ballot in a Cy Young race. In the modern era, where voting often splits between a dominant ace and a strong secondary contender, Misiorowski’s clean sweep reflects the consensus that his season was simply unmatched. His 12 complete games, the most in the league since 2015, also revived a fading art in an era dominated by bullpen specialization, reminding fans and analysts alike of the value of durability and stamina.

Milwaukee’s franchise history adds another layer of significance to Misiorowski’s triumph. The Brewers have produced only one other NL Cy Young winner—Corbin Burnes, who captured the award in 2021 after posting a 1.73 ERA and 234 strikeouts. Burnes’ success helped establish the Brewers as a competitive force in the NL Central, but Misiorowski’s victory signals a new era of pitching excellence for the club. The team’s front office, which invested heavily in analytics-driven scouting and development, can now point to a home‑grown ace as proof that their long‑term strategy is bearing fruit.

Beyond the personal accolades, Misiorowski’s performance has had a tangible impact on the Brewers’ postseason aspirations. With his 18‑5 record, the team sits atop the NL Central and has secured a wild‑card berth, largely on the back of his ability to keep the ball in the park and limit high‑leverage runs. His presence also provides a psychological boost; teammates frequently cite his work ethic and calm demeanor as catalysts for a clubhouse culture centered on resilience. As the playoffs loom, the Brewers will likely lean heavily on Misiorowski, perhaps even extending his role into a short‑turnaround start in the Division Series—a scenario that could test the limits of his durability but also offer a chance to cement his legacy with postseason heroics.

Looking ahead, the implications of Misiorowski’s Cy Young win extend beyond a single season. Contract negotiations are already underway, with the Brewers expected to lock him into a long‑term extension that could make him one of the highest‑paid pitchers in baseball. Moreover, his success may influence how other clubs approach pitcher development, potentially sparking a renewed emphasis on cultivating complete-game starters rather than relying solely on specialized relievers. For Milwaukee fans, the celebration is immediate, but the broader narrative suggests that Jacob Misiorowski is poised to become a defining figure of the modern game, shaping both his franchise’s fortunes and the evolving philosophy of pitching in Major League Baseball.
